title: Linux Network Toolkit: ip, ss, ping, curl, dig, ssh and Firewall Basics
summary: Quick revision notes on inspecting and debugging a Linux host's network. Covers interfaces, sockets and ports, the core debug order, everyday commands, remote access, firewall basics and the common mistakes.

chapters.title: Mental Model and Debug Order
points: Layers: interface with IP (ip) → route to gateway → DNS name resolution (dig) → port reachable (ss, curl) → firewall allows it. Debug bottom-up in that order.
Socket = IP + port + protocol. A service LISTENs on a socket; a client connects from a random ephemeral port (32768-60999 by default on Linux).
Bind address matters: 127.0.0.1 is local only, 0.0.0.0 is all IPv4 interfaces, :: is all IPv6. 'Works locally, fails remotely' usually means a loopback bind.
Core workflow when 'it can't connect': ip addr (have an IP?) → ip route (default gateway?) → ping 8.8.8.8 (internet by IP?) → dig example.com (DNS?) → curl -v (service answers?).

Interview Point: (1) A service works on localhost but not from another host. What do you check? (2) Ping by IP works but ping by name fails. Which layer is broken? (3) What is the difference between a listening port and an open port?

chapters.title: ip and ss: Interfaces, Routes and Listeners
points: ip -br a prints a brief one-line-per-interface view of addresses and UP/DOWN state. ip link shows layer 2: state and MAC.
ip route shows the routing table. 'default via X dev eth0' is the gateway. ip route get 8.8.8.8 shows which route and source IP a packet would use.
ss replaces netstat. ss -tulpn = TCP, UDP, Listening, Process, Numeric. Needs sudo to show processes owned by other users.

ss -tn state established shows live connections. ss -tn 'sport = :443' filters by port. Local Address:Port column shows the bind address, so 127.0.0.1:5432 is local only and *:5432 or 0.0.0.0:5432 is public.

Interview Point: (1) Which command shows what is listening on port 8080 and which process owns it? (2) How do you find which interface and gateway are used to reach an IP? (3) Why did ss replace netstat?

chapters.title: ping, curl, wget and dig in Practice
points: ping -c 4 host sends 4 ICMP echo requests; it shows reachability, packet loss and RTT. ICMP can be blocked, so a failed ping does not prove the host is down.

curl -v URL shows DNS, connect, TLS and the HTTP headers. -I fetches headers only. -s silences the progress meter. -o file saves to a file. -L follows redirects. -k skips cert verification (testing only).
curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"a":1}' URL sends a JSON POST. -w '%{http_code}' prints the status code. --connect-timeout 5 limits a hung connect.
curl vs wget: curl is for single requests and APIs and writes to stdout by default. wget downloads files to disk, resumes with -c and mirrors with -r.

dig example.com A +short gives just the answer. dig @8.8.8.8 example.com queries a specific resolver and bypasses the local one. dig -x IP does a reverse lookup. Record types: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, NS.

chapters.title: ssh, scp and Firewall Basics
points: ssh user@host -p 2222 -i ~/.ssh/key connects with a custom port and key. The private key file must be chmod 600 or ssh refuses it.
~/.ssh/config with Host, HostName, User, Port and IdentityFile entries lets you type just 'ssh alias'. Add ProxyJump bastion to hop through a jump host.
scp file user@host:/path copies up. scp user@host:/path/file . copies down. Use -r for directories and -P (capital) for the port, unlike ssh's lowercase -p. rsync -av is better for repeated syncs.
ssh -L 8080:localhost:80 user@host forwards a local port to the remote side (tunnel). Use ssh -v to debug auth failures. Prefer key auth over passwords.

Interview Point: (1) A firewall allows port 22 but ssh times out vs 'connection refused'. What does each mean? (2) What are the differences between ufw, firewalld and iptables/nftables? (3) How does ssh key auth work?

chapters.title: Common Mistakes
points: Timeout vs refused: 'connection refused' means the host answered but nothing listens on that port (check ss). A timeout usually means a firewall or security group is dropping packets, or a wrong route.
Opening an app port in the host firewall (ufw allow 8080) but forgetting the cloud security group or router. Both layers must allow it, and a service bound to 127.0.0.1 stays unreachable either way.

Firewall rule order and lockout: enabling ufw or setting default deny before allowing SSH (ufw allow 22 first) locks you out of a remote box. iptables rules are first-match and not persistent across reboot unless saved.

Trusting a cached or wrong DNS answer: testing with curl or ping through the local resolver while the record changed. Verify with dig @8.8.8.8 and check the TTL. Also, ping a hostname succeeding does not mean the port is open.
scp -p vs -P, running ss without sudo (no process names shown), and using curl -k in production. Use nc -zv host port to test whether a TCP port is open.

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet
points: Interfaces and routes: ip -br a | ip route | ip route get IP | ip link
Listeners and connections: ss -tulpn (listeners + process) | ss -tn state established | sudo lsof -i :PORT
Reachability: ping -c 4 host | nc -zv host port | curl -v URL | curl -sI URL | curl -w '%{http_code}' -o /dev/null -s URL
DNS: dig example.com +short | dig @8.8.8.8 example.com | dig -x IP | dig example.com MX
Remote and firewall: ssh -i key -p PORT user@host | scp -P PORT -r dir user@host:/path | ssh -L 8080:localhost:80 host | sudo ufw allow 22/tcp; sudo ufw enable; sudo ufw status numbered
